content: The protein known as TES, also referred to as Testin, is the product of the TESS gene, which is located on chromosome 7 in humans (Homo sapiens). TES is a 47 kDa protein consisting of 421 amino acids and is primarily found at focal adhesions. It is believed to play a role in regulating cell motility. TES also functions as a tumor suppressor. The TESS gene is situated within a fragile region of chromosome 7, and its promoter elements are susceptible to methylation. This methylation process inhibits the expression of the TES protein. Domain Organization TES is composed of several domains. The structures of the cysteine-rich domain and the PET domain remain unknown. However, the LIM domains are well-characterized and are known to act as modulators of protein-protein interactions. LIM domains consist of two zinc fingers separated by two hydrophobic amino acids, typically a phenylalanine followed by a leucine. Binding Partners TES does not appear to function as an enzyme. Instead, it mediates and regulates cellular functions through protein-protein interactions. Some of its potential binding partners, such as Zyxin and mENA, are found in focal adhesion complexes. The range of binding partners suggests that TES may play a role in linking actin polymerization to focal adhesion contacts with the extracellular matrix. This hypothesis aligns with observations that GFP-tagged TES localizes to focal adhesions. The linker region and all three LIM domains of TES are capable of binding to Zyxin. Additionally, the N-terminal region of TES, which includes the cysteine-rich and PET domains, interacts with the C-terminal region, indicating that the two halves of TES can interact with each other. Garalov and colleagues proposed that TES exists in two conformational states. In the closed state, the N-terminal and C-terminal halves of TES interact, which obscures the Zyxin-binding site in LIM1. In the open state, the Zyxin-binding site becomes accessible, and the two halves no longer interact in the same manner, if at all. The regulatory mechanism that governs the transition between these two states is not yet fully understood. Phenotype In RNA interference (RNAi) experiments, cells with impaired TES expression exhibited defects in organizing their focal adhesions and actin stress fibers. In gene knockout experiments, transgenic mice lacking both copies of the TES gene showed an increased susceptibility to tumor formation when exposed to a carcinogen. In contrast, mice retaining the TES gene were less susceptible to tumor development. These findings confirm that TES functions as a tumor suppressor gene.
